title: Midweek Musings - August 26, 2026
author: Matthew Justin Hall
summary: In his weekly digest, Biola University provost Matthew Justin Hall combines an original essay adapted from his faculty-conference address with curated, editorialized links to three outside pieces. The original essay argues that a Christian university claiming to care about "the good life" must define it concretely: as the specifically human life (not mere biological or computational existence), as something cultivated through discipline and virtue rather than stumbled into, as inherently shared and resistant to individualist atomization, and ultimately as the Godward life, where Augustine's insight is that flourishing is a received gift of grace rather than an achievement. Hall then curates a professor's confession of being transformed by teaching The Brothers Karamazov for the first time, Joseph Epstein's Commentary reflection on turning ninety and Aristotle's account of friendship, and cultural pieces on the disappearance of vivid color from film and architecture. The digest models Hall's own thesis by treating classical and Christian sources (Augustine, Aristotle, Dostoevsky) as living resources for thinking about formation, aging, and shared life rather than museum pieces.
points: Argues a university claiming to care about 'the good life' must define it in specific terms rather than gesture at the phrase, proposing four concrete claims: human, cultivated, shared, and Godward.

Draws on Augustine's Confessions and City of God to argue flourishing is not self-actualization but a received gift of grace, quoting Augustine that possessing happiness without hope of what is beyond 'is but a false happiness and profound misery.'

Curates a professor's confession of being professionally transformed by finally teaching The Brothers Karamazov, using it to argue teachers must 'transmit the spark of passion' in their own person, not just their material.
Includes Joseph Epstein's reflection on turning ninety and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of friendship, using classical sources to frame aging, loss, and the limits of human companionship.
quotes: Whatever else we are, we are not merely another species of the animal kingdom, and we are certainly not biochemical computers with legs, waiting patiently to be replaced by something more efficient coming down the factory line.
No one falls into it by accident. Happiness is formed, not stumbled into. That pursuit requires intentionality, discipline, and virtue.
Augustine's genius was to see that flourishing isn't an achievement at all. It's a gift of grace, received, not earned.

If any man uses this life with a reference to that other which he ardently loves and confidently hopes for, he may well be called even now blessed, though not in reality so much as in hope. But the actual possession of the happiness of this life, without the hope of what is beyond, is but a false happiness and profound misery.

What I discovered anew in my encounter with The Brothers Karamazov last term was that if you want students to be passionately engaged, not worried about the future, grasping, careerist or disengaged, you must transmit the spark of passion in your deeds, your mien, in your own soul.
